context: A liturgical interjection scattered through the Psalms — likely an instruction to pause and reflect.
definition: A musical or liturgical term whose precise meaning is uncertain, but most likely a directive to pause, lift up, or reflect on what has just been spoken or sung. It appears 71 times in the Psalter and three times in Habakkuk.
significance: Selah is a pause built into scripture itself — a sanctioned silence. Worship is not only spoken but also rests; truth is meant to be sat with before the next line begins.

context: More than the absence of conflict — the deepest blessing one Hebrew could speak over another.
definition: A rich Hebrew noun spanning peace, wholeness, completeness, prosperity, and the integration of all things as they should be. Used as both a greeting and a theological vision of human and cosmic flourishing.
significance: Where English peace is mostly the absence of war, shalom is the presence of flourishing. The biblical hope is not a quiet world but a whole one — relationships restored, justice settled, creation at rest.

context: John takes a Greek philosophical term and identifies it with Christ — the Word made flesh.
definition: Word, speech, reason, or rational principle. In Greek philosophy, Logos was the ordering rationality behind the cosmos. John's prologue claims this Logos became a particular human being in first-century Judea.
significance: John's audacious move bridges Athens and Jerusalem: the rational principle behind reality is not an abstraction but a person. Christ is what God has been saying about himself from the beginning.

context: Distinct from eros and philia — the willed, sacrificial love commanded toward God and neighbor.
definition: The highest of the Greek words for love. Distinct from eros (romantic), philia (friendship), and storge (familial), agape names a love that is chosen rather than felt — a willed orientation toward another's good regardless of merit or response.
significance: Agape reframes love as action, not emotion. It can be commanded — even toward enemies — because it does not require the cooperation of feeling. It is the kind of love God is said to be.

context: The unseen, animating force — present at creation and in the prophets.
definition: A single Hebrew word spanning wind, breath, and spirit. Ruach is the invisible force that gives life — the breath in the lungs, the wind across the wilderness, and the Spirit of God that hovers over the deep.
significance: The same word that names the wind names the Spirit of God — what is unseen and yet undeniably moving. From the breath that hovered over the chaos to the breath that filled dry bones, ruach is the texture of divine presence.

context: Hebrew truth is less a correct proposition and more a steadfastness you can stake your life on.
definition: From the root aman — the same root that gives us amen. Emet names what is firm, faithful, reliable, and trustworthy. It applies to people who keep their word, witnesses whose testimony holds, and a God who keeps covenant.
significance: Truth in Hebrew is closer to fidelity than to factuality. God is described as abundant in hesed and emet — overflowing love and the unshakable reliability that keeps the love from being mere sentiment.

context: The nearly untranslatable word for the love that does not let go.
definition: A Hebrew word combining love, loyalty, and obligation — the steadfast covenant love a faithful partner shows even when the other has failed. Translators reach for compound phrases: lovingkindness, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness.
significance: Hesed is the texture of God's relationship with his people — love that has signed something, that is bound, that keeps showing up. Where ordinary love would walk away, hesed remains.

context: Distinct from chronos — not the ticking clock but the charged, decisive moment.
definition: Where chronos measures sequential, quantitative time — minutes, days, years — kairos names a qualitative moment: the right time, the appointed time, the opportunity that must not be missed.
significance: Scripture insists that history is not only duration but timing. There are moments when the kingdom is at hand and the door swings open. Kairos names the now that the chronos was waiting for.

context: The Greek inheritor of ruach — the Spirit at Pentecost, blowing where it wishes.
definition: The Greek counterpart to Hebrew ruach, carrying the same breadth of meaning across breath, wind, and spirit. In the New Testament it most often names the Holy Spirit and the human spirit's response.
significance: The same dynamic, life-giving breath that hovered over Genesis becomes the wind of Pentecost. Pneuma binds the testaments: the God who created by breathing now empowers the church by the same Spirit.

context: An Aramaic prayer preserved untranslated in the Greek New Testament — the heart-cry of the early church.
definition: An Aramaic phrase preserved in the Greek text without translation. Most likely marana tha — "Our Lord, come!" — though some read it as maran atha — "Our Lord has come." Used as a closing prayer in early Christian gatherings.
significance: Paul did not bother to translate it for his Greek-speaking readers — they already knew the word. Maranatha is the early church's prayer in its native tongue, the longing for the return of Christ left raw and untranslated.

context: Not a formal religious title but the warm, familial word a child would use for a parent.
definition: The Aramaic word for father in its familiar form — closer to papa than to a formal patriarchal title. Used by Jesus in his prayer in Gethsemane and taken up by Paul as the cry the Spirit teaches in the heart of the believer.
significance: Abba reframes prayer as the speech of children. Jesus addresses God in his most agonized hour with the warmest possible word — and Paul claims the same word now belongs in the mouths of those adopted into the family.

context: A word of agreement that stakes the speaker's reliability on what was just spoken.
definition: From the root aman — to be firm, faithful, trustworthy. Used as a congregational response affirming what has been spoken, and uniquely by Jesus as a prefix to authoritative declarations: amen, I say to you.
significance: The final word of the Bible. Amen is the human answer to divine speech — agreement, ratification, the staking of one's life on what has been said. Jesus's strange habit of beginning sentences with it claims the authority to declare truth before it is even uttered.

context: A literal command — "you all, praise Yahweh." The crescendo of the Psalter and the song of Revelation.
definition: A compound: hallelu, the plural imperative of the verb "praise," joined to Yah, a shortened form of the divine name YHWH. Untranslated in most languages because it carries the divine name within itself.
significance: The Psalter does not end with a prayer or a meditation but a command — five psalms shouting praise. Revelation hears the same word in heaven. Hallelujah binds the worship of Israel to the worship around the throne.

context: Jesus draws on a real, infamous valley outside Jerusalem to picture final judgment.
definition: A Greek transliteration of the Hebrew Ge-Hinnom — the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, historically a site of child sacrifice under Israel's worst kings. Jesus uses the name as his most common image for eschatological judgment.
significance: Jesus does not invent hell from abstractions. He points to a literal place outside the city walls — a real ravine with a grim history — and warns that its image is also a destiny. The geography anchors the warning.

context: The rabbinic name for the visible, manifest presence of God among his people.
definition: A post-biblical Hebrew term — not in the Hebrew Bible itself but coined by the rabbis from the verb shakan, "to dwell" — naming the glorious, manifest presence of God: the cloud over the tabernacle, the fire on Sinai, the glory filling the temple.
significance: John's prologue says the Word skenosen — pitched his tent — among us, deliberately echoing the language of God's presence in the tabernacle. Christ is the new Shekinah: the divine presence walking the earth in a body.

translation: I am who I am; the Lord
context: The personal name of the God of Israel — too holy to pronounce.
definition: Four Hebrew consonants — yod, he, waw, he — known as the Tetragrammaton. Given to Moses at the burning bush as "I am who I am." The vowels are not preserved; Jewish tradition reads Adonai or HaShem aloud rather than utter the Name itself.
significance: The name God gives himself is a kind of refusal of definition — being itself, the One who is. Christianity hears Jesus take this name on his own lips in the seven I AM sayings of John's Gospel, claiming an identity unmistakable to his Hebrew hearers.

context: The most common Hebrew word for God — and grammatically plural.
definition: A plural form of the Hebrew el — god, deity. Used in the Hebrew Bible both of pagan gods (in the literal plural) and of the God of Israel (with singular verbs). The plural form has been variously read as a plural of majesty, a relic of older Semitic religion, or a hint of inner divine plurality.
significance: The very first word of action in scripture — 'in the beginning, Elohim created' — pairs a plural noun with a singular verb. Hebrew faith insists on one God but speaks of him in a word that has always carried a quiet excess.

context: The Hebrew title spoken aloud where the divine name YHWH was written.
definition: A plural form of adon (lord, master) used exclusively of God. In Jewish practice, Adonai is read aloud whenever the unpronounced divine name YHWH appears in the text — a verbal substitute that protects the holiness of the Name.
significance: Most English Bibles render the divine name as 'LORD' in small capitals — a translation tradition that follows the Jewish practice of saying Adonai where YHWH is written. The Lord whom Christians confess is the same Lord whom Israel addressed as Adonai.

context: The opening word of Israel's central confession of faith.
definition: Imperative form of the verb shama — to hear, listen, obey. From its first word the central Jewish prayer takes its name: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai Echad — Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one.
significance: Hearing, in Hebrew, is never merely auditory. To hear is to attend, to respond, to act. The Shema is therefore not only a creed but a posture: a daily ordering of life toward the God whose first word to his people is listen.

context: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible — and, more deeply, the divine instruction itself.
definition: From the verb yarah — to throw, to point — and so to point the way, to instruct. Torah is the divine instruction given to Israel, narrower in name (the five books of Moses) and broader in scope (the whole shape of God's teaching).
significance: English 'law' is a thin translation: torah is closer to guidance than to legislation, more parental than legislative. It is given not to constrain freedom but to teach the people of God how to be human.

context: The seventh day, set apart at creation and commanded into Israel's life.
definition: From the verb shavat — to cease, desist, rest. The Sabbath is the weekly day on which Israel ceases from work in imitation of God's rest on the seventh day of creation.
significance: Sabbath is the first thing in scripture that God calls holy. It is a rhythm built into time itself — a refusal of the lie that human worth is measured in productivity. The Sabbath, Jesus said, was made for man.

context: The Hebrew title behind both Messiah and (in Greek) Christ.
definition: From the verb mashach — to anoint with oil. Kings, priests, and occasionally prophets were anointed in Israel; the title came in time to point beyond them to a coming, definitive anointed one — the Messiah.
significance: Christ, the title we now use as if it were a surname, is simply the Greek of Mashiach. Every time the word is said it carries the long ache of Israel waiting for the one God promised to anoint.

context: The Hebrew word too often flattened into the abstract English 'soul.'
definition: A living, breathing creature — the throat, the appetite, the life. Used of animals as well as humans, nephesh names a whole embodied life, not a disembodied component of one.
significance: Hebrew anthropology is not a soul housed in a body but a body that became, by the breath of God, a living nephesh. Salvation, in scripture, is therefore the redemption of the whole person — not the escape of a soul from one.

context: The visible weight of God's presence in the Hebrew Bible.
definition: From the root meaning heavy. The kavod of someone is their weightiness, their reputation, the substantive presence they carry. God's kavod is the visible, weighty manifestation of his presence — fire on Sinai, cloud in the tabernacle, glory filling the temple.
significance: Glory in scripture is not abstract radiance but a kind of weight — something heavy enough to press the priests out of the temple. Kavod is what makes a place where God has come unsafe to enter casually.

context: The Hebrew word translated 'repentance' — closer to coming home than to feeling sorry.
definition: From the verb shuv — to turn, to return. Teshuvah is the act of turning back: turning away from the path you were on and turning back toward God.
significance: Repentance in Hebrew is not primarily an emotion but a direction. It is the prodigal's walk back up the road. Teshuvah names what the Father runs out to meet.

context: The Hebrew word for a person whose life is rightly ordered toward God.
definition: From the root tzedek — righteousness, justice. A tzaddik is one whose life conforms to the right order, who keeps faith with God and with neighbor.
significance: Noah is called tzaddik; so is Abraham; so, by extension, are all who walk faithfully with God. The prophet Habakkuk wrote the line — 'the righteous shall live by his faith' — that Paul made central to the gospel a thousand years later.

context: The Hebrew word for covenant — the deepest category in biblical thought.
definition: A binding agreement, oath, or pact. Brit is not a casual contract but a formal, ratified commitment between two parties — often sealed with blood. The Bible understands God's relationship with his people as a series of such covenants.
significance: From the rainbow with Noah to the new covenant in Christ's blood, the Bible is structured as a story of brit. The English 'testament' (as in Old and New) is itself a translation of this word.

context: The Hebrew word for the long horizon — both backward and forward.
definition: Originally what is distant or hidden in time — the age beyond view. Olam can name the distant past, the unending future, or the whole of the world that lies within time. In later Hebrew it also comes to mean 'world.'
significance: Eternity, in Hebrew, is less a timeless absolute than an unending horizon. God is El Olam — the God of the age, of every age, from olam to olam. The new heavens and the new earth are an olam habba, the world to come.

translation: the grave, the realm of the dead
context: The Hebrew Bible's quiet name for the place of the dead.
definition: The shadowy underworld where all the dead, righteous and wicked, descend in the Hebrew Bible. Less a place of torment than a place of silence — gravity, weakness, distance from the praise of God.
significance: Sheol is the Old Testament's reticence about the afterlife — the dead are there, somewhere, and that is mostly all that is said. The hope of resurrection emerges slowly in the prophets and the Psalter, and unfolds fully only in the New Testament.

context: The cry of the crowds at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem.
definition: A compound: hoshia (save) and na (please, we pray). Originally a desperate cry for help — found in the Hallel psalm sung at Passover — by the first century it had become a shout of triumphant petition during festival processions.
significance: The crowd that lined the road into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday was praying as it shouted. Hosanna is both adoration and request — a recognition that the one entering on a donkey was, in fact, the one come to save.

context: The actual name of Jesus, in his mother tongue.
definition: A late form of the Hebrew name Yehoshua — Joshua — meaning 'the Lord saves.' Yeshua was a common Jewish name in the first century. The Greek transliteration is Iesous; the Latin, Iesus; the English, Jesus.
significance: The name Mary heard from the angel was not Jesus but Yeshua — a name already heavy with the story of an earlier man who had led Israel into the promised land. Now another would lead them, the Gospel of Matthew explains, by saving them from their sins.

context: The Greek title behind every use of the name 'Christ.'
definition: The literal Greek of the Hebrew Mashiach — the anointed one. In the Septuagint and the New Testament, Christos translates Mashiach. What looks in English like a second name of Jesus is in fact his title: Jesus the Christ, Jesus the anointed one.
significance: To say 'Jesus Christ' is to make a claim, not state a name. The whole hope of Israel for an anointed king, priest, and prophet — the long line of mashiachs across the Hebrew Bible — is gathered up in those two words: Jesus is the Christos.

context: The early church's word for the return of Christ.
definition: Literally being-alongside or being-present. Used in the wider Greek world of the official arrival of a king or emperor in a city — the parousia. In the New Testament it most often names the coming of Christ in glory.
significance: Parousia is both arrival and presence. The early church did not wait for an event so much as a Person. The same word names what we are waiting for and the One who, in the Spirit, is already here.

context: The Greek word that becomes 'church' in English.
definition: Literally those called out — from ek (out of) and kaleo (to call). In secular Greek it named a civic assembly; in the New Testament it names the assembly of those summoned by God.
significance: The church, before it is an institution or a building, is a gathering. It is the assembly of people called out and called together by Christ. Ekklesia keeps that original meaning audible behind the much-used English word.

context: The richly physical Greek word translated 'salvation' in the New Testament.
definition: From soter, savior. In wider Greek it could mean rescue from any peril — shipwreck, disease, military defeat. The New Testament uses it of God's deliverance: from sin, death, judgment — and toward wholeness, healing, life.
significance: English 'salvation' has narrowed to a transaction at the end of life; soteria is much wider. It includes healing of the body, restoration of relationships, deliverance from oppression — the whole life rescued by Christ.

context: A single Greek word holding what English splits between faith and faithfulness.
definition: Trust, confidence, reliability — both the trust placed in someone and the trustworthiness of the one trusted. Pistis can mean a person's faith and another person's faithfulness; the New Testament uses both.
significance: Faith in scripture is not credulous belief but personal trust — placed in someone reliable enough to bear it. Pistis joins both sides of the relationship: my trust and God's trustworthiness.

context: Christian hope as confident expectation, not wishful thinking.
definition: The expectation of good to come — confident, not anxious. Distinct from the cautious modern 'hope so,' elpis is closer to settled assurance grounded in the character of the one who promised.
significance: Christian hope is not optimism in the face of evidence but trust in a future already secured by the resurrection. Elpis is an anchor — fastened, the letter to the Hebrews says, in the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.

context: The defining word of Pauline theology.
definition: Favor, grace, gift — and the gratitude such a gift evokes. In secular Greek a charis was an act of patronage; in Paul it becomes the unearned favor of God toward sinners, freely given.
significance: Grace in Paul is not merely a softening of God's justice but the very ground of the gospel. Christianity is held up, the New Testament insists, not by what we manage but by what we have been given. From charis comes 'charity' — and 'eucharist,' the great thanksgiving.

context: The Greek word that holds both personal righteousness and social justice in one breath.
definition: From dike, justice or judgment. Dikaiosyne names both the moral integrity of a person and the right ordering of a society. Greek did not divide these the way English does.
significance: When Jesus blesses those who hunger and thirst for dikaiosyne, he means both inner uprightness and outer justice. The two cannot finally be separated. Righteousness is a community that has been put right.

context: The central theme of Jesus's preaching — the kingdom of God.
definition: The reign or rule of a king, and so by extension the realm in which that king rules. Translators reach for both senses: 'kingdom' for the realm, 'reign' for the active rule of God.
significance: The kingdom in Jesus's preaching is not a place but a happening — the active reign of God breaking in among his people. It is at hand, in the midst of you, both now and not yet. To pray 'your kingdom come' is to pray for that reign to be unmistakable.
